1.0.m: frequented by the foremost of Brahmins devoted to vows and observances and intent on the emergence of Brahmā,

1.1.m:
purified by the gaze of Brahmā, the teacher of the three worlds, adorned with rays,
pleasant with widespread enjoyment, removing misfortune—may the water of Puṣkara purify you.

To the Sūta seated in solitude, the disciple of Vyāsa of great intellect,
named Lomaharṣaṇa, or to Ugraśravas, he said:

"Dear child, having gone to the hermitages of the sages, when they ask
briefly about dharmas, speak at length that which you have heard from me.

All the Purāṇas obtained by me from Vedavyāsa, my son,
have been narrated to you; proclaim them at length to the munis,

and how the Lord Himself was questioned at Prayāga by the best of munis,
and how those munis desirous of dharma were instructed by Him when questioned.

Desiring a holy region, [they were told] by the Lord who wished for their welfare:
'With a fine navel, divine form, moving in truth, of auspicious stride,

this matchless wheel is rolling. Untiringly,
follow behind it with restraint; you will reach the state that is beneficial.

Where the rim of the rolling wheel of dharma shatters,
that country is to be regarded as holy.' Thus spoke the Lord Himself.

Having spoken thus to all the sages, He became invisible once more.
Where the rim shattered in a whirlpool of the Gaṅgā,

the sages then offered sacrifice in Naimiṣa with an extended sacrificial session.
Going there, speak to those who question you about doubts regarding dharma."

Then Ugraśravas, having gone, knowing knowledge, approached the best of sages,
greeted them respectfully, bowed down with folded hands,

and the wise one gladdened those sages with prostrations.
And those sacrificers, along with the members of the assembly, delighted with the great-souled one,

assembled together and offered him proper worship.
The sages said:
"Whence have you come, Sūta? From what country have you arrived here?

And tell us the reason for your coming, you who possess the splendour of the gods!"
The Sūta said:
"I was commanded by my father, the wise disciple of Vyāsa:

'Go and attend upon the munis; what they ask you, tell that to them.'
Let the revered ones tell me what tale I shall narrate:

A Purāṇa, or legendary history, or duties of various kinds?"
The best of sages heard that sweet speech of his;

then their desire to hear the Purāṇa arose,
seeing that disciple, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, to be highly trusted and learned.

In that sacrificial session, the head of the assembly, skilled in all scriptures,
wise, named Śaunaka, a master in the knowledge of the Araṇyaka,

taking up that intention of theirs, desiring to hear about dharmas, said to him:
"By you, O Sūta of great intellect, the blessed one, the best knower of Brahman,

For the sake of legendary history and the Purāṇas, you have thoroughly served Vyāsa;
you have milked his auspicious intellect which was the resting-place of the Purāṇas.

Now these foremost of Brahmins desire to hear the Purāṇa,
O one of great intellect; you should make them hear it.

Indeed, all these great souls of various clans have gathered;
let these expounders of the Veda hear their respective shares declared in the Purāṇas.

When this extended sacrificial session is completed, recite to these munis;
relate the Padma Purāṇa to all of them, O great-minded one!

How was the lotus born, and how indeed did Brahmā come to be there?
How was creation made by him when he arose? Tell us that accurately."

Questioned thus, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa then replied to them with auspicious speech,
subtle and endowed with reasoned principles, he spoke:

"I am pleased, I am favoured by your prompting here,
by knowers of the Purāṇas devoted to all dharmas, for the sake of the Purāṇa.

As it was heard and renowned, I will tell you all of that.
This is the eternal duty of the Sūta, seen by the virtuous:

The preservation of the genealogies of gods, sages, and kings of immeasurable splendour,
and praises of the great-souled ones.

Those who expound the Veda are seen in legendary history and the Purāṇas;
for no entitlement to the Vedas is observed in the case of a Sūta.

During the ongoing sacrifice of the son of Vena, the great-souled Pṛthu,
the Māgadha and the Sūta praised that lord of men.

Then, being pleased, a boon was given to the two by the great-souled king:
to the Sūta, the Sūta country, and to the Māgadha, Magadha.

Born at that pressing of soma, one is known here as a Sūta.
When the sacrifice of Indra commenced while Bṛhaspati was united with the planets,

in that sacrifice of Indra relating to Bṛhaspati, the Sūta was born there,
when the oblation of the guru, mixed with the disciple's hand, was overwhelmed.

From the pouring out of place, that mixture of castes arose
wherein they were born of a kṣatriya from the womb of a brahmin woman.

They are proclaimed as dissimilar by their difference from the former [original Sūta].
For this is the intermediate duty of a Sūta, one living off the field.

My authority over the Purāṇas has been ordained here by the Brahmins;
perceiving this duty, I have been questioned by you expounders of the Veda.

Therefore, I shall speak properly on earth the Purāṇa worshipped by sages.
The mind-born daughter of the ancestors went to the son of Vasu;

and, cursed by the ancestors, she entered the belly of a fish,
like the kindling-stick of fire, the cause of an auspicious birth.

From her, the pure-souled great sage was born from Parāśara.
Having bowed to that blessed one, the truthful creator,

the ancient Puruṣa, follower of the word of the Veda,
having assumed the guise of a mortal, Viṣṇu of praised self,

and who, as soon as he was born, approached the Veda along with its compilation,
by whom, turning the churning-rod of intellect in the ocean of revelation,

light was produced in the world, the moon that is the Mahābhārata.
If these three—the Bhārata, the sun, and Viṣṇu—did not exist,

then what would be the state of the world, blinded by the darkness of ignorance?
Know that Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa is Lord Nārāyaṇa;

for who else other than the Lotus-eyed One could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
From him, an expounder of the Veda, I heard the Purāṇa,

from the omniscient one worshipped in all the worlds, of blazing splendour.
The Purāṇa was remembered first by Brahmā among all the scriptures,

supreme among all worlds, producing all knowledge,
achieving the three aims of life, holy, extending to one billion [verses].

And when the worlds were completely [overwhelmed], Keśava, in the form of a horse,
brought back the Vedas at the command of Brahmā;

the limbs, the four Vedas, and the extent of Purāṇas and logic—
the entire scripture having been stolen by the asura and taken for himself,

He took it back in the form of a fish at the beginning of the kalpa in the watery ocean.
Remaining within the water, the Lord spoke all of this;

and hearing it, the Four-faced One proclaimed the Vedas to the sages.
Then occurred the beginning of all the scriptures and of the Purāṇa.

Seeing that in time the Purāṇa would not be grasped, the Lord then,
in the form of Vyāsa, that Brahmā, for the sake of compilation in every age,

sang it in each Dvāpara age to the extent of four hundred thousand [verses];
then, dividing it into eighteen parts, it was revealed in this world of mortals.

Even today in the worlds of the gods it extends to one billion [verses]; / here that very [text] is presented concisely in four hundred thousand.
2
I shall proclaim the greatly meritorious Purāṇa called the Padma, / having fifty-five thousand [verses] and endowed with five sections.
3
There, first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and after that the Bhūmikhaṇḍa; / then the Svargakhaṇḍa, and after that the Pātālakhaṇḍa;
4
and fifth after that is celebrated the supreme Uttarakhaṇḍa. / This very great lotus arose, consisting of which is the universe;
5
because it is based on that account, it is therefore called the Padma. / This spotless Purāṇa is immaculate with the glorification of Viṣṇu,
6
which the god of gods, Hari, indeed proclaimed to Brahmā long ago, / [and] which was told earlier by Brahmā precisely to Marīci.
7
This very Padma [Purāṇa] Brahmā spoke in the world; / and that which is the refuge of all beings is called the Padma by the wise.
8
That Padma is recited here as fifty-five thousand [verses]; / it is proclaimed in five sections, abridged by Vyāsa.
9
The first section is the Puṣkara, where the Virāṭ himself was born; / the second is the Tīrtha section, the refuge of all the hosts of planets.
10
In the third section are treated the kings who give abundant sacrificial fees; / and in the fourth is proclaimed the history of lineages.
11
In the fifth the truth of liberation and all fundamental truths are spoken. / In the Puṣkara is the ninefold creation of all things made by Brahmā,
12
of deities, sages, and also another, the creation of the ancestors; / in the second are the mountains and the seven continents with their oceans;
13
in the third is the creation of Rudra and likewise the curse of Dakṣa; / in the fourth is the origin of kings and the narration of all dynasties;
14
in the last is the status of beatitude and the recitation of the teachings on liberation. / All this in this Purāṇa I will tell you, O twice-born.
15
This is pure, a treasure of renown; this is very dear to the ancestors; / this is ever for the joy of the deity, and this destroys the great sins of men.
16
Thus in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the first Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, [ends] the first chapter on the descent of the Purāṇa.

Chapter two.
18
Sūta said:
19
I bow to the master of all worlds, of the entire universe, / who assumes this disposition in the form of creation, knowing the Pradhāna;
20
the maker of the world, knowing the truth of the world, having resorted to yoga, knowing yoga, / he created all beings, moving and unmoving.
21
Desiring to know the Purāṇa narrative, I go for refuge to that all-pervading, unborn Viśvakarman, / the lord of consciousness, the witness of the world.
22
Having bowed with a focused mind to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lord of the mountains [Śiva], / with meditative composure to Indra, the guardians of the world, and the Sun;
23
and to the greatest of sages, the great-souled Vasiṣṭha; / to the sage Jātūkarṇya, who has radiant penance, who was his pupil and eye;
24
having bowed to that blessed creator, Vedavyāsa, / the ancient person who follows the words of Bhṛgu,
25
from him, the proclaimer of the Veda, all-knowing, / revered in all the worlds, of blazing splendour, I heard the Purāṇa.
26
The unmanifest which is the cause, eternal, consisting of being and non-being— / it creates from the Mahat to the specific elements; such is the conclusion.
27
Earlier, within the golden egg, was the supreme birth of Brahmā; / and the covering of the egg was by water, and that of water by fire,
28
of that [fire] by air, of air by space; that was enclosed by the origin of elements; / and the origin of elements by the Mahat, and the Mahat is enclosed by the unmanifest.
29
And the manifestation of the worlds is described within that very egg; / the manifestation of rivers and of mountains is described;
30
the description of the Manvantaras in brief and of the Kalpas; / the description of the dissolution in the tree of Brahmā and the creation of Brahmā’s progeny;
31
and the progression of the Kalpas, and likewise the establishment of the universe; / and the sleeping of Hari on the waters, and then the lifting up of the earth;
32
the tenfold succession of births of Keśava due to Bhṛgu's curse; / the arrangement of the cosmic ages and the division of all the stages of life;
33
and the division of the heavenly stations of mortals going to heaven; / and the origin of beasts and birds is proclaimed;
34
likewise the etymological explanation of the Kalpa, the taking up of self-study; / then the secondary creations made with intention by Brahmā are spoken of;
35
and three others without intention; likewise he fashioned the worlds; / and the emergence of Bhṛgu and the others from Brahmā's mouths;
36
the interval between two Kalpas is spoken of, and the junction between two creations; / and the description of the creation of progeny by the sages beginning with Bhṛgu;
37
and the attainment of Brahmanhood by the Brahmin-sage Vasiṣṭha is proclaimed; / and after that, the account of the Manu Svāyambhuva;
38
the emission by Nābhi is told, and of the great-souled Rajas; / and the glorification of the continents, oceans, and mountains;
39
the divisions of continents and their inclusion in the seven oceans; / they are described with the extent of yojanas, as well as those who dwell there;
40
and their regions along with rivers and mountains; / the continents beginning with Jambūdvīpa are encircled by the seven oceans.
41
Inside the egg are these worlds, and the earth with seven continents; / the course of the sun and moon, and of the planets and the stars;
42
and through the power of Dhruva the good and bad fortune of creatures is proclaimed; / the solar chariot was fashion by Brahmā himself for a purpose;
43
the blessed sun, fashioned by him, moves forth; / the motion of the chariots of the sun and others proceeds from Dhruva alone;
44
and the dolphin constellation was fashioned, in whose tail Dhruva is situated; / and at the end of creation is dissolution, and at the end of dissolution is creation;
45
of the deities, the sages, Manu, and the host of ancestors; / it is impossible to speak of it at length, so it is stated concisely;
46
of the past and future [beings] together with Svāyambhuva; / the proclamation of the gods and lords of progeny in the Manvantaras;
47
occasional, elemental, and absolute— / thus a threefold dissolution of all beings is considered to be ordained;
48
drought caused by the sun, and the terrible fire of universal destruction; / and the clouds of universal deluge, as well as the night of the great-souled [Brahmā];
49
the characteristic of the twilight is indicated, especially that of Brahmā; / and the description of the seven worlds of beings;
50
and by me are recounted here the Raurava and other hells for the sinful; / the determination of the transformation of all living beings;
51
and the secondary creation of Brahmā, and the description of the dissolution of all; / and in Kalpa after Kalpa the destruction even of great beings;
52
and having correctly counted and understood the impermanence of Brahmā, / and the wickedness of pleasures, and the hardship of worldly existence,
53
and the rarity of liberation, seeing fault through detachment; / having abandoned the manifest and unmanifest, existence rests in Brahman;
54
from seeing manifoldness he becomes well-established, and then he turns towards that; / then, having transcended the three afflictions, free from form, unstained,
55
having attained the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing from anywhere. / Thus the comprehensive summary of the authoritative work has been described,
56
wherein are proclaimed the transformations of the creation and dissolution of the universe, / and the activity of beings, and the fruits of renunciations.
I shall proclaim the highly meritorious Purāṇa named Padma, / consisting of fifty-five thousand [verses] accompanied by five sections.
Therein, at first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and after that the Bhūmikhaṇḍa; / after that the Svargakhaṇḍa, and next the Pātālakhaṇḍa.
And the fifth is celebrated as the excellent Uttarakhaṇḍa. / This very great lotus emerged, of which the universe is made;
because it is based upon that account, it is therefore called Padma. / This spotless Purāṇa is immaculate with the glorification of Viṣṇu,
which Hari, the god of gods, indeed proclaimed to Brahmā formerly, / and as much as was formerly declared by Brahmā to Marīci,
that very same Padma Purāṇa did Brahmā indeed speak to the world. / And because it is the refuge of all beings, it is called Padma by the wise.
That Padma Purāṇa is recited here as fifty-five thousand [verses]; / it is proclaimed in five parts, through an abridgment made by Vyāsa.
The first part is the Puṣkara part, where Virāj himself was born; / the second is the part on holy sites, the support of all the hosts of planets.
The third part takes up the kings who gave abundant sacrificial gifts; / and the history of lineages is celebrated in the fourth.
In the fifth, the principle of liberation and all fundamental principles are expounded. / In the Puṣkara part, the ninefold creation of all beings was brought about by Brahmā,
as well as the creation of the deities, the sages, and another of the ancestors. / In the second part are the mountains, the seven continents, and the oceans.
In the third is the creation of Rudra, and likewise the curse of Dakṣa; / in the fourth is the origin of kings and the narration of all lineages.
In the final part is the establishment of beatitude and the proclamation of the scripture on liberation. / All this in this Purāṇa I will relate to you, O twice-born ones.

1.1.m:
This is purifying, a repository of renown; this is dearest to the ancestors; / and this is always for the pleasure of the god; this destroys great sins for men.

I bow to the lord of all worlds, of the entire universe, / who, knowing the primordial nature, assumes this state in the form of creation.

The maker of the worlds, knowing the reality of the worlds, relying on yoga, conversant with yoga, / created all beings, unmoving and moving.

Desiring to know the ancient narratives, I go for refuge to that all-pervading lord, / unborn, maker of all things, lord of consciousness, witness of the world.

Having bowed with focused mind to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Lord of the Mountain, / and in deep concentration to Indra, the guardians of the quarters, and the Sun,

and to the greatest among sages, the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, / to his speaker, of shining ascetic power, Jātūkarṇya, who possesses insight,

and having bowed to that blessed creator, Vedavyāsa, / the ancient Person, who follows the word of Bhṛgu—

from him, the expounder of the Veda, all-knowing, revered in all worlds, / of radiant splendor, I heard the Purāṇa.

That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of being and non-being, / creates [everything] beginning with the cosmic intellect down to particular objects: this is the definitive conclusion.

1.1.m:
and how at Prayāga the lord himself was questioned by the foremost sages, / and those sages desiring dharma were instructed by Kṛṣṇa—

all this has been related according to the truth, O best of the twice-born, / as the incomparable world-order of sages ever devoted to dharma,

which was formerly spoken by Brahmā to the great-souled Pulastya, / and then declared by Pulastya to Bhīṣma at Gaṅgādvāra.

It brings prosperity, fame, long life, and the destruction of all sins, / particularly its recitation, hearing, and retention in memory.

This Purāṇa was revealed in proper order by the Sūta, / which was formerly spoken at length by Brahmā among the brahmins.

One who with senses subdued should study it, understanding a single quarter properly, / has studied the entire Purāṇa—of this there is no doubt.

A twice-born who knows the four Vedas with their auxiliary limbs and the Upaniṣads, / and who knows the Purāṇa, is more learned than he.

One should amplify the Veda with legendary history and the Purāṇas;
the Veda fears a person of little learning, thinking, 'He will cheat me.'

Having studied even a single chapter spoken by the Self-born one himself, / having encountered misfortunes, one is liberated and attains the desired goal.

1.1.m:
Because it relates the ancient tradition (purā), it is known as the Purāṇa. / He who knows its etymology is freed from all sins.

The ṛṣis said to the Sūta: "How did the venerable ṛṣi Pulastya, / the mind-born son of Brahmā, meet with Bhīṣma,

whose sight is difficult to obtain by men laden with sin? / This is a great wonder, O Sūta: how was the sage,

a mighty being, propitiated by a kṣatriya? Tell us that, O highly intelligent one. / What kind of penance was done by him, or what other observance was performed,

by which the brāhmaṇa sage was pleased, and so spoke to him / a section, half a section, or the whole?

In what place and how the venerable ṛṣi Pulastya was seen— / tell us that, O fortunate one; we are ready to listen."

The Sūta said:
Where the illustrious Gaṅgā, bringing benefit to the virtuous, / having split the mountain, rushed forth with speed, purifying the worlds—

at the great sacred ford Gaṅgādvāra, Bhīṣma, devoted to the ancestors, / wishing to attend [upon the sages], remained for a very long time in a vow of the great,

for fully one hundred years with supreme concentration, / meditating on the supreme Brahman, performing his ablutions at the three times of day.

1.1.m:
As the great-souled one propitiated the Pitṛs and the gods with the daily recitation of the Veda / and emaciated himself, the divine Grandfather was pleased.

Brahmā said to his son Pulastya, the best of the ṛṣis: / "Go to Devavrata Bhīṣma, the hero born of the Kuru lineage;

turn him back from his penance, and tell him the reason for it. / The illustrious one is engaged in devotion, meditating on the Pitṛs.

Whatever desire is in his mind, fulfill it without delay." / Hearing the words of the Grandfather, Pulastya, the best of sages,

came then to Gaṅgādvāra and spoke these words to Bhīṣma: / "Choose a boon, may you be blessed, whatever is in your mind!
The divine Grandfather himself is pleased with your penance, O hero. / Sent by Brahmā, I shall grant you the desired boons."
Bhīṣma, hearing those words bringing joy to the mind and ears, / opened his eyes and saw Pulastya standing before him.
Bowing to that best of sages with a prostration of all eight limbs, / he spoke, having bowed down, touching the earth with all his limbs:

Today my birth has borne fruit, and this day is very auspicious,
for here your feet, worthy of worship by the world, have been seen by me.
The fruit of my penance has been obtained, since the revered lord has been seen by me, / especially as a giver of boons, arrived at the riverbank.
This seat has been prepared by me; please be seated, it is made comfortable. / And in an offering-vessel of palāśa wood, with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, flowers, kuśa grass,
mustard seeds, curds, honey, barley, and milk— / this eightfold offering was indeed prescribed by the sages of old."
Hearing these words of that Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor, / the venerable ṛṣi Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, sat down.
Delighted, the revered lord accepted the seat together with water for the feet / and the offering-vessel, pleased by that good conduct.

Pulastya said:
"You are truthful, generous in nature, true to your promise, a lord of men, / modest, friendly, forgiving, and valiant in punishing enemies;
you know dharma, you are grateful, compassionate, pleasant in speech, / an honorer of the venerable, wise, devoted to the brahmins, and affectionate toward the virtuous.
I am ever pleased with you, dear child, who are devoted to prostration. / Speak, O fortunate one; I shall tell you the account."

Bhīṣma said:
"O revered one, in what time did the revered, all-pervading Brahmā abide / when he made the creation of the gods and others in the beginning? Tell me.
Or how does the revered Viṣṇu maintain [the world]? And how was Rudra fashioned? / How were the ṛṣis and the gods created by that great-souled one?
How was the earth made, how the sky, and how were these oceans created? / How were the continents, mountains, villages, forests, and cities?
The sages, the Prajāpatis, and the foremost Seven Ṛṣis; / the castes, the wind, the ancient abode, the gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
the holy places, or the rivers, the planets and stars beginning with the sun— / as the revered lord created them, tell me that in detail."

Pulastya said:
Higher than the highest, the supreme, the supreme Self, the Grandfather, / devoid of form, color, and the like, and free from qualifying attributes,
free from decay and destruction, from transformation, growth, and birth, / and devoid of all qualities—he alone truly shines forth.
He is everywhere equal, dwelling as the incomparable one; / contemplating [all], he is proclaimed by the wise under the form of Brahman.
Bowing to him—the secret, supreme, eternal, unborn, imperishable, immutable, / and abiding in the form of Puruṣa and in the form of Time—
I shall explain how he brought about creation, / when formerly the lord of the universe arose from his lotus bed.
Produced by the manifestation of the guṇas at the time of creation, O king of men, / the Mahat [became] threefold: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
Surrounded by the principle of pradhāna, together with the seeds and the like, / the ego is threefold: vaikārika, taijasa, and bhūtādi (which is tāmasa).
This threefold ego arose from the principle of Mahat, / along with the five subtle elements and the sense faculties, together with the faculties of action.
Earth, water, light, air, and ether— / I shall describe each in its essential nature in proper order.
The element-origin [egoism] enveloped the ether, whose subtle element is sound. / Then ether, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch;
and this is strong wind, whose property is considered to be touch. / But ether, whose subtle element is sound, enveloped the subtle element of touch.
Then wind, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of form. / Light is indeed that wind's form; it is said to have the property of form.
Wind, having the nature of touch, enveloped the subtle element of form. / And light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste.
From that waters arise; they enveloped the subtle element of form. / And the waters, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of smell.
From that arises the solid mass [earth], whose property is considered to be smell. / They say the senses are of the fiery type; the ten deities are of the transformational [type].
The mind is the eleventh here; the deities are known as born from transformation. / Skin, eye, nose, tongue, and the ear here is the fifth;
their function is considered to be the apprehending of sound and the rest. / Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals are the fifth among them;
evacuation, craft, movement, and speech are their functions, in reverse order. / Ether, wind, fire, water, and earth,
endowed, O hero, with properties like sound and the rest, each successive [having more]— / they are known as calm, terrible, and deluded, and are therefore called specific elements.
Possessing diverse powers and remaining separate, they were unable, / without combination, having not united completely, to create creatures.
Having come together through mutual connection and mutual reliance, / characterized by a single aggregate, having attained complete unity,
and because of being presided over by the spirit and by the grace of the unmanifest, / those beginning with the intellect down to the specific elements produce the egg.
It expanded in due course like a water bubble. / In it, Janārdana, whose nature is unmanifest, assumed a manifest form;
Brahmā stood by himself in the form of Brahman. / Meru became its inner membrane, and the mountains its outer membrane;
the oceans were the amniotic fluid of that great soul. / In it were the continents, the oceans, and the assembly of luminous worlds.
Within that egg, O hero, were [the worlds] together with gods, demons, and humans. / Surrounded on the outside by water, fire, wind, ether, and the element-origin,
the egg is surrounded by tenfold [layers]; the element-origin likewise by the intellect, / and the intellect, O king, along with all of them, is enveloped by the unmanifest.
Surrounded by all these envelopes, and joined with all elements, / it is like the coconut fruit—a seed [enclosed] by outer layers.
Brahmā himself engages in the creation of the universe; / and he protects the creation in each age, as long as the kalpa unfolds.
The lord Janārdana alone receives those names— / he who enjoys sattva, possesses properties, is the deity of immeasurable valor.
At the end of the kalpa, he manifests an excess of tamas and assumes a terrible form; / O best of kings, exceedingly frightful, he consumes all beings.
And having consumed all beings when the world is turned into a single ocean, / bearing the form of all, he sleeps on the couch of the serpent.
Awakened, he whose form is assumed performs creation once again. / Because of performing creation, preservation, and dissolution, he consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
As creator, he creates himself; as Viṣṇu, he protects what is to be protected; / and as destroyer, the lord himself dissolves [it].
Earth, water, fire, wind, and ether— / he alone is the lord of all beings, for he is all-formed and imperishable.

Knowing the earth was underwater, submerged in the deluge of waters, / Prajāpati reflected, wishing to accomplish its rescue.

Assuming then the form of Viṣṇu, capable of bearing the immense earth by his own splendor, / and other forms such as the fish and tortoise, he entered the form of a boar.

Resorting to a form composed of the Vedas and sacrifices for the preservation of the world, / the steadfast, all-pervading Supreme Self, Prajāpati, stood firm.

Then the bearer of the earth entered the water, into the receptacle of waters. / Seeing him come down to the subterranean realm, the goddess,

the earth, bowing down and humbled in devotion, praised him. / The Earth said: / 'Homage to you, the source of all beings! Homage to you, the Supreme Self!

Deliver me today from this [abyss]; formerly I arose from you. / Homage to you, O Supreme Self! Homage to you whose essence is the cosmic person!

Homage to you who are the unmanifest source and manifest form, and who have become Time! / You are the creator of all beings, you are the protector, you are the destroyer.

1.1.m:
You who are the supreme Brahmā at the beginning of creation, assuming the forms of Viṣṇu and Rudra, / having swallowed everything when the universe became a single ocean,

you alone, O Govinda, lie [upon the waters], contemplated by the wise. / None knows that supreme form of yours.

The denizens of heaven worship that form which you assume in incarnations. / Having revered you, the Supreme Brahman, seekers of liberation have attained liberation.

Indeed, without worshipping Vāsudeva, who can attain liberation? / Whatever form can be grasped by the mind, whatever can be perceived by the eyes and other senses,

and whatever can be discerned by the intellect—all that is your form. / I consist of you, I have you as my support, I was created by you, and I have taken refuge in you.

Therefore, indeed, this world calls me Mādhavī.' / While he was thus being praised by the earth, the bearer of the earth,

sounding like the chants of the Sāma Veda, the glorious one, grunted with a deep rumbling. / Then, raising the earth with his tusk, the great boar, with eyes like blooming lotuses, / rose up from the underworld like a great dark mountain resembling the petal of a blue lotus.

As he rose, the wind from his mouth struck the lotus-dwellers resting in Janaloka, / the faultless sages beginning with Sanandana, and made them repeatedly an abode of purity.

As the great boar rose, tearing open the earth, his belly moist with water, / and shaking his body composed of the Vedas, the sages nestled between his bristles were delighted.

'O Supreme Lord among rulers of men, Keśava, master bearing mace, conch, sword, and discus! / You are the Lord, the cause of origin, destruction, and maintenance; there is no other supreme abode.

The Vedas are in your feet, the sacrificial post is your tusk, the sacrifices are in your teeth, and the sacred revelations are in your mouth; / the sacrificial fire is your tongue, your hairs are darbha grass; O Lord, you alone are the sacrificial Person!

O one of unequalled power, the space between heaven and earth is filled by your body alone, / as is this entire world; be present, O all-pervading Lord, for the welfare of the universe!

You alone are the Supreme Self; there is no other, O Lord of the universe.

This is your majesty, by which this [world] of mobile and immobile things is pervaded. / This entire universe is of the nature of knowledge; yet the unwise,

Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu departed, and the all-pervading Lord created the gods and others. / First, an unconscious creation consisting of darkness appeared from him:

obscurity, delusion, extreme delusion, gloomy darkness, and blind darkness; / this fivefold creation emerged as the great-souled one meditated.

It was devoid of light within and without, enveloped in nature, consisting of immovables; / because immovable things are called primary, this is spoken of as the primary creation.

Seeing that creation ineffective, the Lord thought of another. / As he contemplated, the creation of animals (tiryak-srotas) arose.

Because its course of movement is horizontal, it is known as tiryak-srotas. / They are known as beasts and the like, largely full of darkness and devoid of discernment,

taking wrong paths, imagining themselves to possess knowledge while in ignorance, / egotistical, conceited, comprising twenty-eight types, / illumined within, all of them mutually veiled.

Thinking that also to be ineffective, another [creation] arose as he meditated; / the third was the upward-coursing (ūrdhvasrotas), full of sattva, moving upward.

Abounding in pleasure and delight, unveiled within and without, / illumined both within and without, they are therefore known as ūrdhvasrotas.

1.1.m:
Satisfied in spirit, the third is traditionally remembered as the creation of the gods. / When that creation was accomplished, joy arose in Brahmā.

Then he meditated on another, an excellent and effective creation, / knowing those that originated from the primary creation and others to be ineffective.

As he meditated thus, contemplating truth, / there appeared from the unmanifest the downward-coursing creation (arvāksrotas), which is effective.

Because they proceed downwards, they are called arvāksrotas. / They have much illumination, but are heightened in tamas and rich in rajas.

Therefore, they abound in suffering and act repeatedly; / they are illumined within and without; they are humans and are effective [agents].

The fifth is the creation of grace (anugraha), and it is arranged in four ways: / through error, accomplishment, incapacity, and satisfaction.

They do not know what has passed or what is present; / that of beings originating from the elements is called the sixth creation.

They are all acquisitive, distinctly differentiated, / inclined to promptings and mutterings; they are to be known as the elemental beings.

In this manner these six creations have been related, O best of kings;
the first was the creation of Mahat, and the second was that of Brahmā.

the second is remembered as the creation of the subtle elements and bhūtas, / and the third creation is known as the modified ego and the organs of sense.

Thus this primary creation arose, preceded by intellect.
The fourth is the principal creation, and the immovable beings are indeed considered principal.

And that which is called the horizontal stream is said to be the animal birth. / Then the sixth, of those of upward stream, is regarded as the creation of the gods.

Then the seventh is the creation of those of downward stream; that is the human one. / The eighth is the grace creation; it is characterized by sattva and by tamas.

These five are the secondary creations, while three are known as primary. / The ninth is known as the Kaumāra, both primary and secondary.

These nine creations of Prajāpati have been declared to you, / primary and secondary, the fundamental causes of the universe.

While the Lord of the Universe creates, what else do you wish to hear? / Bhīṣma said: / The creations of the gods and others have thus been told by you, O master, in brief;

I desire to hear it in detail from you, O best of excellent sages! / Pulastya said: / Imbued with their deeds, both auspicious and inauspicious,

not freed by that discernment, they were gathered together at the dissolution. / The creatures, ending with the immovable and beginning with the gods, O king, are fourfold;

as Brahmā was making creation, they were born as his mind-born [offspring]. / Then, wishing to create the four—gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans—

he applied himself to these waters. / Then from the liberated soul of Prajāpati, evil-minded ones were born.

As he wished to create, the asuras were first born from his hips. / He then cast off that foul body consisting of mere tamas.

That body cast off by him, O best of kings, became the night. / Desiring to create while residing in another body, the gods then found delight;

abounding in sattva, they arose from the mouth of Brahmā, O king. / That body, too, was cast off by him, and it became the day, largely filled with sattva.

Therefore, the asuras are powerful at night, and the deities by day. / Then he assumed another body, consisting solely of sattva.

As he thought of himself as a father, the ancestors were born of him. / Having produced the ancestors, that Lord then cast off that body as well.

And that cast-off [body] became the twilight, the state between day and night. / Then he assumed another body, consisting of mere rajas.

Men were born, characterized by an excess of mere rajas, O best of Kurus. / Prajāpati quickly cast off that first body as well;

1.1.m:
and it became moonlight, which is called the early twilight. / At the arrival of moonlight, men are strong, and likewise the ancestors,

O best of kings; therefore, they prevail at twilight time. / Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these are the four [bodies] of the Lord,

the bodies of Brahmā which are bases for the three qualities. / Then he assumed another body consisting of mere rajas.

Then hunger arose in Brahmā, and anger was produced by it; / emaciated with hunger in the darkness, the Blessed One then created.

Deformed and desiring to eat, they ran toward the Lord. / Those who said, "Protect him!" became rākṣasas;

the others who said, "Let us devour him!" became yakṣas. / Seeing them, the hair of the Creator fell out in extreme terror;

and having fallen from the head, they climbed onto the head again. / From crawling (sarpaṇa) they became serpents (sarpa); from having fallen (hīna) they are called ahis.

Then, by the angry Creator, wrathful beings were made; / they were tawny in color, fierce spirits, eaters of flesh.

While he was sucking the earth, the gandharvas arose from him at that moment; / drinking speech, they were born, and therefore they became gandharvas.

the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra he created from his west mouth. / The twenty-one-fold stoma, the Atharvan, and the Aptoryāma,

the Ānuṣṭubha meter, and the Vairāja he created from his north mouth. / High and low beings were born from his limbs.

Having created the gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans, Prajāpati, / that Grandfather, created again at the start of the kalpa:

yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise hosts of apsarases, / siddhas, kinnaras, rākṣasas, lions, birds, deer, and serpents,

and whatever is imperishable and perishable, stationary and moving: / all that the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the all-pervading first maker, created then.

Whatever deeds those beings took on in their former creation, / those very deeds they take on when created again and again.

Hurtful or harmless, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, true or false— / imbued with that, they assume it; therefore, that is what pleases each.

Among sense objects, elements, and bodies, the Lord, / the Creator himself, produced variety and application.
The name and form of beings, and the elaboration of duties, / he made in the beginning from the words of the Veda for the gods and others.
The names of the sages, as they are heard in the Veda, / and appropriate functions for others as well, he assigned.
Just as the various signs of the seasons are seen each in its turn / as the seasons change, so too the states of being in the ages and other periods.
He performs this kind of creation again and again at the start of a kalpa; / desiring to create, endowed with power, impelled by the power to be created.
Bhīṣma said: / The downward-streaming one, which is the human creation, was mentioned by you; / O Brahmin, tell me in detail how Brahmā created it,
how he created the castes and qualities, O great sage, / and what duty is prescribed for them, beginning with the brahmins; let that be told!
Pulastya said: / Formerly, as Brahmā meditated on sattva, desiring to create offspring, / offspring abounding in sattva were born from his mouth, O best of Kurus.
Others abounding in rajas arose from the chest of Brahmā; / likewise, from his thighs arose those abounding in both rajas and tamas.

From his two feet Brahmā created other creatures, O best of the Kurus,
all of them dominated by darkness; and thereafter this system of four castes.
brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, O best of kings, / arisen from the feet, thighs, chest, and mouth.
Brahmā made all this for the performance of sacrifice; / the four castes, O great king, are the supreme means of sacrifice.
The gods are gratified by sacrifice, and men by the shedding of rain; / sacrifices of dharma are gratified, since they are the cause of welfare.
They are performed by men who are always devoted to good deeds, / free from perverse conduct, virtuous, and treading the path of the good.
From human existence men attain heaven and final liberation, O king; / and to whatever realm they desire, to that they go, O lord of men.
Those beings created by Brahmā in the arrangement of the four varnas, / were thoroughly pure and of upright conduct, O best of kings,
devoted to living as they wished, free from all afflictions, / of pure inner consciousness, pure, and spotless through the performance of dharma.
And when their minds were pure, and Hari was seated in their pure hearts, / they perceived pure knowledge, through which that realm called Brahman is seen.
Then that [influence] which is of the nature of Time, which is spoken of in Viriñci's [creation], / causing a descent into saṃsāra, exceedingly terrible and of little substance,
arising from darkness and greed, became the seed of adharma / among the creatures, O king of kings, producing passion and the rest.
From that, their natural perfection did not arise in full measure, / O king, nor the other eight perfections such as subduing others,

When they were all diminished and wickedness increased,
those creatures then became afflicted with suffering born of the assault of dualities.
Therefore they built fortresses: arboreal, mountainous, aquatic, / and also desert fortresses, as well as cities, market towns, and the like.
And in those cities and other settlements they built houses according to rule, / for the alleviation of afflictions such as cold and heat, O highly intelligent one.
Having made this defense against cold and other elements, those beings then / made means of livelihood and manually acquired skill born of labor.
Paddy, barley, wheat, small grain, sesame, / Italian millet, kovidāra, kodo millet, and cīnaka;
black gram, mung bean, lentil, broad bean, horse gram, / pigeon pea, chickpea, and hemp—these are declared to be seventeen.

Thus these are the species of cultivated plants, O king;
and the sacrificial plants, cultivated and wild, are fourteen.

śyāmāka millet, wild rice, round peas, and gavedhuka grass, / and bamboo grains are declared, likewise monkey-grass, O king.
These are indeed remembered as fourteen herbs, cultivated and wild; / likewise for the accomplishment of sacrifice, they are an excellent cause.
And these, together with sacrifice, are the supreme support of beings; / therefore the wise who know both higher and lower perform sacrifices.
The performance of sacrifices day by day, O best of monarchs, / produces benefit for men who desire its fruits.
And for those whom this drop of time's creation fell upon, O highly intelligent one, / he established limits according to place and qualities,
and the dharmas of the varnas and the āśramas, O best of the upholders of dharma, / and the realms for all varnas who properly maintain their dharmas.
The realm of Prajāpati is remembered for the Brahmins, O king; / the realm of Indra for Kṣatriyas who do not turn back in battle;
the realm of the Maruts for Vaiśyas who follow their own duty; / the realm of the Gandharvas for the Śūdra castes who are engaged in service.
And that realm which is remembered for the eighty-eight thousand / ascetics with sublimated sexual energy is the very same for those dwelling with a teacher.
And that realm which is remembered for the Seven Rṣis is for forest dwellers; / that of Prajāpati is for householders; that known as Brahman's is for renunciants.
The deathless realm is for yogins, the supreme state of Brahman; / for those who are exclusively devoted, always striving, meditating yogins—
theirs is that supreme realm which the sages behold. / Moving to and fro, the moon, sun, and other planets return;
even today, those wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa do not return. / Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the dreadful Asipatravana, Kālasūtra, and Avīci / are declared to be the realm of revilers of the Veda,
of those who obstruct sacrifices, and of those who abandon their own duty. / Then, as he was meditating, mind-born offspring were born to him.
Together with the bodily sense organs produced from that body, / the knowers of the field arose from the limbs of that wise one.
They all arose, whom I mentioned before, / beginning with the gods and ending with immobile things, situated in the realm of the three guṇas.
Thus the beings, both immobile and mobile, were created. / When all those beings of the wise one did not multiply,
he then created other mind-born sons equal to himself: / Bhṛgu, myself, Pulaha, Kratu, and Aṅgiras,
Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha—these nine mind-born sons / are determined in the Purāṇa as the nine Brahmās.
And those such as Sanandana who had been created before by the Creator / did not cling to the worlds, unconcerned with producing offspring;
for they were all endowed with wisdom, free from passion, and devoid of envy. / When they were thus indifferent toward the creation of the world,
a great anger arose in the high-souled Brahmā, capable of burning the three worlds. / Arising from his wrath, blazing with garlands of flames,
the radiant light of Brahmā then burned the entire three worlds. / From his forehead, contracted in a frown and blazing with anger,
Rudra was then born, shining like the midday sun, / with a body half-woman and half-man, fierce, having a huge form.
Having said to him, 'Divide yourself,' Brahmā then vanished. / Being addressed thus, he divided himself into femaleness and maleness;
and the lord divided his male form into ten and one; / and into gentle and non-gentle, calm forms, and his femaleness
he divided into many parts with forms black and white. / Then Brahmā made himself, who had existed beforehand, as the self-born lord,
the progenitor Manu, O king, for the role of Prajāpati; / and that woman Śatarūpā, whose sins had been dispelled by asceticism,
the lord Svāyambhuva Manu took as his wife. / And from that man the goddess Śatarūpā bore
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, and [two daughters] named Prasūti and Ākūti. / In ancient times he gave Prasūti to Dakṣa, and Ākūti to Ruci;
the Prajāpati [Ruci] took her, and from the two of them Dakṣiṇā was born, / and then a son, the glorious Yajña—a twin pair to the couple.
And by Dakṣiṇā twelve sons were born to Yajña; / they are known as the Yāma gods under Svāyambhuva Manu.
And Dakṣa likewise begot twenty-four / daughters upon Prasūti; hear their names properly from me:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Medhā, Kriyā, / Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapu, Śānti, Ṛddhi, and Kīrti as the thirteenth.
Lord Dharma took these daughters of Dakṣa as his wives. / The eleven fair-eyed daughters who remained, younger than these,

Khyāti, Satī, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā,
Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and Svadhā:

Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, the sage Aṅgiras,
I [Pulastya], Pulaha, and Kratu, the best of sages,

Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Agni, and the ancestors, in order,
took as wives these maidens, beginning with Khyāti, O best of kings.

Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; Lakṣmī to Bala; Dhṛti to her son Niyama;
Tuṣṭi to Saṃtoṣa; and Puṣṭi brought forth Lobha.

Medhā gave birth to Śruta; Kriyā to Daṇḍa, Naya, and Vinaya;
Buddhi to Bodha; and Lajja to her son Vinaya, while Vapu gave birth to her son [Vyavasāya].

She gave birth to Vyavasāya; Śānti brought forth Kṣema;
Ṛddhi gave birth to Sukha, and Kīrti to Yaśas: these are the sons of Dharma.

From Kāma, Nandī gave birth to a son, Harṣa, the grandson of Dharma.
Hiṃsā was the wife of Adharma, and to him she bore Anṛta,

And the maiden was Dishonesty; from those two arose Fear and Hell,
and Deceit and Torment, a pair and indeed a duality.

Of those, Māyā produced Mṛtyu, who snatches away living beings;
and from Vedanā, through Raurava, was born Duḥkha.

From Mṛtyu were born Vyādhi, Jarā, Śoka, Tṛṣṇā, and Krodha.
All these, having sorrow as their culmination, are remembered as the characteristics of Adharma.

They have neither wives nor sons; they are all celibate.
These terrible forms belong to Brahmā, O son of an excellent king;

they constantly serve as the cause of dissolution for this universe.
I shall now describe the creation of Rudra, as Brahmā carried it out.

At the beginning of the kalpa, as he meditated on a son equal to himself,
there appeared in the lap of the Lord a youth of blue and red hue.

Crying out with a loud voice and running about, O best of kings,
the god said to him as he was crying: "Why do you weep?"

He then replied to Prajāpati: "Give me a name!"
"Because of your crying (rodana) you are named Rudra; do not weep, summon patience!"

Addressed thus, he wept again seven times;
thereupon the Lord gave him seven other names,

and he established eight places for his eight forms:
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, and Paśupati, O king,

Bhīma, Ugra, Mahādeva—thus spoke the Grandfather:
the sun, water, the earth, fire, wind, space,

an initiated brahmin, and the moon: these are their bodies in order.
Being of such nature, that Rudra obtained Satī as his wife.

Because of Dakṣa's anger, Satī abandoned her own body.
She then became the daughter of Himavat, born of Menā, O best of kings.

The blessed Bhava, having asked for her, married her once again.

He, upon whose aroused anger the animate and inanimate universe falls into terror—

Mahendra, descending in haste from the elephant's shoulder,

propitiated the stainless sage Durvāsas.
Even when being propitiated by him at that time with prostrations,

'I shall not forgive! What is the use of speaking much, O Śatakratu?'
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed; the king of the gods too

mounted the elephant Airāvata again and departed for Amarāvatī.
From that time on, the three worlds, together with Śakra, became devoid of fortune.

Sacrifices were not performed, ascetics did not practice penance,
and gifts were not given; the world was as if destroyed.

When the three worlds were thus utterly devoid of fortune and bereft of vitality,
the Daiteyas and Dānavas prepared an army against the gods.

Defeated by the Daityas, the gods headed by Indra,
with Agni at their head, went for refuge to the glorious Grandfather.

When told properly by the gods, Brahmā spoke thus to the deities,
and went to the northern shore of the milk ocean together with the gods.

1.1.m:
Having gone there, the blessed Grandfather addressed Vāsudeva:
'Arise, O Viṣṇu, swiftly work the welfare of the deities!

Without you, they have all been repeatedly conquered by the Dānavas.'
Addressed thus, the lotus-eyed one, the Puruṣa, the Supreme Being,

seeing the gods reduced to an unprecedented condition, said:
'O gods, I shall bring about the augmentation of your splendor.

I tell you what should be done by you; let this be done, O gods:
having brought all herbs together with the Daityas to the milk ocean,

making Mandara the churning rod and making Vāsuki the churning rope,
let the nectar of immortality be churned, O gods, while I stand by as your helper.

First speaking with conciliation to the Daiteyas concerning that task,
[tell them:] 'You too will be equal enjoyers of the fruit here.'

And as the ocean is being churned there, whatever nectar of immortality is produced,
from drinking that, you will become strong and immortal.'

[he gave to others]. 'I will act in such a way that the enemies of the thirty [gods] / will not obtain the nectar of immortality, O gods, and will only share in affliction.'

Having been addressed thus by the god of gods, all the gods then,
having made an alliance with the Asuras, strove for the nectar of immortality.

1.1.m:
The gods, daiteyas, and dānavas brought all herbs / and cast them into the water of the milk-ocean, which shone as clear as autumn clouds.

Making Mount Mandara their churning rod and Vāsuki their churning cord, / they then began to churn swiftly for the nectar, O best of kings.

All the gods stood together where the tail was; / the daityas were placed by Viṣṇu at the front part of Vāsuki's body.

By his breath-wind and by his fire, their luster scorched, / all the asuras became devoid of energy, O you who have the splendor of an immortal.

And by that very wind from his breath and by the clouds / that showered rain at the region of his tail, the gods were then refreshed.

In the middle of the milk-ocean, the blessed Brahmā, best of knowers of brahman, / and Mahādeva of great splendor dwelt on Viṣṇu's back.

Seizing Mandara with his arms like a lotus, that scorcher of foes, / having then made a chain, held Mount Mandara.

Stationed in the midst of the forces of the gods and the dānavas, / in the middle of the milk-ocean, was the blessed Lord Hari himself in the form of a tortoise.

first Surabhi, the cow supplying offerings, arose, worshipped by the gods. / Then the gods and the dānavas rejoiced, O highly wise one.

All their minds were distracted, and their eyes became fixed in wonder. / While the siddhas in the sky were thinking, “What is this?”, then

arose the goddess Vāruṇī, her eyes rolling with intoxication, / causing whirlpools, and stumbling at every step from it.

Wearing a single garment, her hair disheveled, red-cornered and unblinking her eyes, / [she said:] “I am the goddess who bestows strength; let the dānavas take me.”

Thinking Vāruṇī to be impure, the asuras then rejected her; / the daityas then seized her, and from being taken, she became surā.

In the churning arose the Pārijāta tree, the splendor of the gods, the tree of the Nandana garden; / and then groups of apsarases endowed with the qualities of beauty and generosity.

Sixty crores were then born, common to both gods and dānavas; / all of them were previously made common by meritorious deeds.

Then the cool-rayed moon arose, the bestower of delight to the gods. / The god Śaṅkara requested: “Let him be an ornament for my matted locks;

there is no doubt he will be: this moon is taken by me.” / And Brahmā consented to it, for the adornment of Hara.

Then the terrible Kālakūṭa poison arose, / and all the dānavas, along with the gods, were afflicted by it.

the groups of immortals headed by Indra, the vidyādharas and great serpents, / the dānavas and great daityas, and the rākṣasas together with the guhyakas,

desired the maiden. Then Brahmā spoke: / “O Vāsudeva, take her indeed, for she is given by me.

Both the gods and the dānavas have been forbidden by me here; / I am pleased indeed with your freedom from greed in this action.”

That Śrī was then addressed by Brahmā: “O goddess, go to Keśava; / having obtained as husband him whom I have given, rejoice for eternal years.”

As all the gods looked on, she went to the chest of Hari; / then, having reached his chest, she spoke words to the god:

“I must never be abandoned, O god, always carrying out your command; / I will dwell upon your chest, O beloved of the whole world.”

Then, looked upon by Lakṣmī standing on Viṣṇu's chest, / the gods, O king of kings, immediately attained supreme bliss,

while the daityas, having turned away from Viṣṇu, fell into supreme agitation; / the dānavas, headed by Vipracitti, were abandoned by Lakṣmī.

Then those daityas seized what was in Dhanvantari's hand, / that nectar, for those daityas were possessed of great strength and joined with sin.

1.1.m:
Alluring them by illusion, Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a woman, / approached and said to the dānavas: “Let the water pot be given to me;

having come under your control, I will stay in your house.” / Seeing that woman endowed with beauty, the loveliest in the three worlds,

the daityas, whose minds were struck by lust, courting her of beautiful body, / gave the nectar to her, and then they watched before her.

Taking the nectar from the dānavas, he then gave it to the gods; / then the hosts of gods headed by Śakra drank that nectar.

With weapons raised and swords drawn, the daityas attacked them; / but the nectar having been drunk, the army of the daityas was then conquered by the powerful [gods].

Being slain, they fled in all directions and entered Pātāla; / then the gods, filled with joy, having bowed down

to the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, went to heaven as before. / From that time on, those terrifying dānavas became lustful after women;

cursed by Kṛṣṇa, they went to Rasātala. / Then the sun, of bright radiance, proceeded on his own path,

and the blessed consumer of oblations flared high with lovely brilliance; / and the minds of all beings were then turned to righteousness.

1.1.m:
The three worlds were endowed with prosperity and protected by Viṣṇu. / But those gods were then addressed by Brahmā, the sustainer of the world:

“For your protection Viṣṇu has been appointed by me, / and Umā's lord, the ruler of the gods; they will provide your welfare,

for they, being constantly worshipped, bring about your security; / therefore these two will always be protective and granters of boons.”

Having spoken thus, the blessed Lord went to his own abode. / When the god, the grandfather of all the worlds, had vanished from sight,

and when Śakra had gone to the realm of the gods, Hari and Śaṅkara / immediately reached their own realms, the gods' dwelling and Kailāsa.

Then the three worlds were protected by the king of the gods. / In this way, highly fortunate Lakṣmī arose from the milk-ocean.

Later, this eternal one arose from Khyāti and Bhṛgu; / she arose alongside Śrī and the great sage Bhṛgu.

And a city of her own name was previously founded on the bank of the river / Narmadā, O great king, approved by Brahmā.

Lakṣmī, having entrusted her own city along with its key to her father, / went to the world of the gods, and returning, she asked for it again.

When she requested it again, however, the city was not returned out of greed. / Because she did not receive it from Bhṛgu, she then spoke to Keśava:

1.1.m:
“I have been humiliated by my father; my city has been seized. / Snatch that city from his hands and bring it back yourself.”

Going to him, the lotus-eyed god, bearer of the discus and mace, / gently said to Bhṛgu: “Give the city to your daughter.

Let both the key and the lock be given through your grace.” / Bhṛgu, angered, replied to him: “I will not give up the city.

That city is not Lakṣmī’s, O god; it was built by myself. / Lord, I will never give it up; cease your objection, Keśava!”

The god spoke to him once more: “Surrender that city to Lakṣmī. / By my word, O great sage, it must certainly be abandoned by you.”

Then Bhṛgu, overcome with rage, said to Keśava: / “O virtuous one, out of partiality toward your wife, you oppress me now.

You will take ten births in the world of men, O Madhusūdana; / through separation from your wife, you will experience sorrows.”

Thus Bhṛgu, exceedingly irascible, pronounced a curse upon him. / And Viṣṇu, the great-souled one, again pronounced a curse upon him:

“You shall never obtain delight caused by offspring, O best of sages!” / Having bestowed the curse upon that sage, he went to the world of Brahmā.

1.1.m:
Beholding the lotus-born [Brahmā], the divine Keśava said this: / “O Lord, that son of yours, Bhṛgu, is exceedingly irascible.

Without cause, I was cursed by him: ‘You will take ten births among human beings; / from that, numerous sorrows [shall arise for you],

a pain born of separation from your wife that destroys strength and manly valor.’ / Abandoning this world, I shall lie upon the great ocean.

Let there be no invocation or rituals in all divine ceremonies [for me].” / While that god was speaking thus, Brahmā, the guru of the worlds, then

uttered this praise to pacify Viṣṇu: / “By you this world was created; a lotus issued from your navel, / and there I was born, subject to your control, O Keśava.

You are the protector of all worlds; you are the creator of the universe, O Lord. / You must not abandon the three worlds—this alone is my boon [asked of you].

With the desire to benefit the worlds, you yourself will undertake / ten births among men; no one had the power to curse you.

Who is this Bhṛgu? How could he have the power to curse you, Janārdana? / Honor the Brahmins always; the Brahmins are your very own body.

Resort to yogic sleep; sleep in the ocean of milk, O Lord. / At the time of need, I will awaken you again, O Mādhava.

1.1.m:
Lord, Śakra, strengthened by your power, / slayer of enemies, will perform all deeds through a portion of yourself.

Protecting the three worlds, he will execute your command.” / Praised in this manner, Viṣṇu then said this to Brahmā:

“I will do all this that you instruct me to do, O Lord.” / The god vanished from sight, and Brahmā did not recognize him.

When the divine Viṣṇu had departed, Brahmā, grandfather of the worlds, / the sovereign origin of all worlds, once again performed creation.

Seeing him, Nārada, best among those skilled in speech, said: / “The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet; / all-pervading, touching the earth, he stands ten fingers beyond it.

What has been and what is to come—you are all of it, since / from you, dear one, this whole universe has come to be and will come to be.

From you arose the sacrifice of all-offering, the clotted butter, and the two kinds of sacrificial animals; / the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born from you alone.

From you the sacrifices were born; from you horses and tusked elephants; / cows were produced from you; from you goats and sheep, as well as wild beasts, were born.

1.1.m:
From your mouth the brāhmaṇas were born, and from you the kṣatriyas arose;
the vaiśyas were born from your thighs, and the śūdras emerged from your feet.

From your two eyes came the sun, from your ear the wind, from your mind the moon; / the vital breath arose from the inner cavity, and from your mouth fire was born.

From your navel the sky arose, and the heavens came forth from your head; / the directions from your ear, the earth from your feet—from you all this has come into being.

Just as an immense banyan tree resides within a tiny seed, / so has he created the entire universe while you served as the seed.

Just as the banyan tree arising from the seed-sprout stands forth / and attains vast expansion, so does the universe in creation from you.

For just as a banana tree is seen as nothing other than its skin and leaves, / so this universe, situated in you, O Lord, is seen as nothing other [than you].

That gladdening power resides in you, coexisting with you alone;
the power causing delight, torment, and their mixture does not exist in you who are devoid of qualities.

Homage to you who are distinct, who are single-formed, who are all beings! / You are the manifest, primordial matter, the cosmic person, the universal ruler, and the sovereign.

You are within all, being all entities, the all, assuming the form of all; / everything has arisen from you; therefore, homage to the self of all!

1.1.m:
Since you are the self of all, the lord of all, abiding in all beings, / what then shall I tell you? You know all that lies in my heart.

Whatever desire I had, O god, has been fulfilled by you. / My ascetic penance was well performed and fruitful, since you, O Lord of the universe, have been seen.”

Brahmā said: / “That is the fruit of your austerity, my son, that I have now been seen by you. / Indeed, the sight of me never becomes fruitless in this world, O Nārada.

Therefore, choose a boon according to your own desire. / Everything comes to pass, dear one, once I have entered one’s field of vision.”

Nārada said: / “O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, you abide in everyone’s heart. / What can be unknown to you, my master, of that which was desired by my mind?

Creation was made by you, just as it was witnessed by me, O omnipresent one; / through that, wonder arose in me upon seeing the divine sages and the Dānavas.”

Pulastya said: / Brahmā, the divine lord of heaven and father of Nārada, was pleased; / he granted a boon to Nārada: “You shall be the highest among sages.

By my grace, you will be fond of amusing quarrel-tales; / and your movement shall be unimpeded in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld.

A sacred thread, a strap hanging as a meditation band, / a parasol, and a lute shall serve as your ornaments, O sinless one.

In the presence of Viṣṇu, of Rudra, and likewise of Śakra, O Nārada, / and in the continents of earthly kings, you will always attain delight.

You shall be a teacher of the social orders; this boon has been given by me to you. / Dwell as you please, my son, being honored by the gods in heaven.”

“How did the auspicious Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, cast off her body? / And for what reason was Dakṣa's sacrifice destroyed by Rudra?

This is my curiosity, O Brahmin: how did the divine Maheśvara, / the glorious enemy of Tripura, fall under the sway of wrath?”

Pulastya said: / “Formerly at Gaṅgādvāra, O Bhīṣma, Dakṣa undertook a sacrifice. / There the hosts of gods and asuras, the ancestors, and the great sages

assembled, filled with joy—all the gods accompanied by Vāsava, / the serpents, Yakṣas, Suparṇas, as well as climbing plants and medicinal herbs.

The venerable Kaśyapa, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, / the Pracetases, Aṅgiras, and Vasiṣṭha of great ascetic heat [came there].”

Having prepared an even altar there, he arranged the fourfold priesthood: / Vasiṣṭha was the hotṛ priest there, and Aṅgiras the best of adhvaryu priests.

Thus, when the sacrifice was underway and the fires were being offered into, / observing that supreme and auspicious abundance prepared of food and drink,

a great altar measuring ten yojanas in every direction across the ground / was constructed there by all of them gathered together.

Seeing all the gods, headed by Śakra, at the sacrifice, the auspicious Satī / then spoke these entreating words to the Prajāpati:

Satī said: / "Mounted upon Airāvata, Śatakratu, king of the gods, / has arrived accompanied by his wife Śacī; Śatakratu has taken up his dwelling here.

He who is the restrainer of sinners, the lord of the unrighteous according to dharma, / is seen to have come here together with his wife Dhūmorṇā.

And the divine lord of aquatic creatures, Varuṇa, who causes the world to prosper, / Pracetas, has arrived in the pavilion here accompanied by his wife Gaurī.

The god who is lord of all yakṣas, son of the sage Viśravas, / the lord of wealth, has arrived here accompanied by his wife Sahadevī.

He who is the mouth of all the gods and dwells in the belly of living beings, / for whose sake the Vedas arose—he has approached the sacrifice.

That Nirṛti, lord of rākṣasas, who was appointed as guardian of the quarter, / he too, O father, has come here to the sacrifice together with his wife.

He who bestows lifespan in this world, fashioned of old by Brahmā, / named Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna,

surrounded by his host of forty-nine— / that prajāpati, the god Vāyu, has arrived at the sacrifice.

He whose self is twelvefold, overseer of the planets, the eyes of the world here, / who indeed protects the whole universe, who is the refuge of the gods,

the lord of longevity, of forests, and of days, / the husband of Saṃjñā, the sun who purifies the worlds, has arrived here.

Born in the lineage of Atri, the renowned king of the twice-born, / producer of joy to the eyes, protector of the worlds on the earth's surface,

Hearing that news, Rudra, intensely grieved by the death of his wife, / resolved firmly to destroy the sacrifice as the gods were watching here.

A crore of gaṇas were commanded, and likewise the grahas, the Vināyakas, / the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, for the destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice.

Having gone there, they conquered and destroyed all the gods at the sacrifice. / When the sacrifice was destroyed, Dakṣa, then bereft of zeal and energy,

approached terrified and spoke to the god of gods, Pinākin: / "You were not known by me, O god, as the lord and ruler of the gods.

You are the sovereign of this universe; all the gods have been conquered by you. / Show mercy, O Maheśāna, and turn back all the gaṇas!"

To the one seated on a bull, to Soma, to the ender of the time of sacrifice! / Obeisance to the one whose garment is the skin of the quarters! Obeisance to you of intense splendour!

To the Brahman, to the one whose body is Brahman, friendly to Brahmins, unmeasured, / to the lord of the mountain, to the lord of the gods, to Īśāna, obeisance, obeisance!

To Rudra, the counter-thunderbolt, to Śiva, the destroyer, / to the ruler of suras and asuras, to the lord of ascetics, obeisance!

To the smoke-coloured, fierce, deformed, sacrificer of dreadful form, / to Virūpākṣa, to the one of ominous eyes, to the thousand-eyed, indeed, obeisance!

To the shaven-headed, to the fiercely shaved, to the bearer of the excellent skull-staff, / to the form of ancestral offerings, to the sacrificial oblation, to the destroyer of all, obeisance!

Compassionate to devotees exceedingly, praised with the Rudra recitation, / to the formless, the beautiful-formed, the maker of a hundred forms,

to the five-faced, the auspicious-faced, the moon-faced, obeisance, obeisance! / To the giver of boons, the worthy of boons, to the tortoise and the deer,

having playful curls and crest, carrying a water-pot, / having the universe as name, then to the universal, to the lord of the universe, obeisance, obeisance!

O Three-Eyed One, O slayer of Tripura, let protection be granted to us / who have surrendered with mind, speech, body, and sentiment, O Maheśvara!"

Thus praised at that time by Dakṣa, who had taken refuge in bodily form, / [the god] was then greatly propitiated by this divine hymn.

"The entire fruit of your sacrifice has been granted by me, O Prajāpati; / for the attainment of all desires, you shall obtain the unexcelled fruit."
