Thus addressed by the Blessed One, having bowed to the lord of gods, / he then went to his own abode right before the eyes of the gaṇas.

Grieved by the sorrow for his wife, the god then stayed at Gaṅgādvāra, / meditating upon that Satī: "Where indeed has my beloved gone?"

To him overcome by grief, Nārada came into the presence of Bhava: / "That Satī of yours, O lord of gods, the wife dear as life, who died,

she was born as the daughter of Himavat from the womb of Menā; / she, knowing the Veda and the meaning of the Veda, has taken another body."

Hearing this, the god then in meditation saw her descended [on earth]; / having made himself accomplished in his purpose, the god then remained [content].

Having attained her youth, the goddess was married once again. / Thus indeed has been told, O Bhīṣma, how the sacrifice was destroyed of old.

1.6.m: Bhīṣma said: / "Of the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, / tell me in detail this origin according to rule, O guru."
Pulastya said: / "Creation of the ancients is said to have occurred through intention, sight, and touch; / after Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, creation arose from sexual union.
Just as he created it, listen in that very way, O descendant of Kuru. / When, as he was creating divine sages, gaṇas, and pannagas,
the world did not attain increase, then through sexual union / Dakṣa begot a thousand sons upon Asiknī.
Seeing those illustrious ones assembled, desiring to create diverse offspring, / Nārada spoke to the Dakṣaputras, the Haryaśvas:
"Knowing the full extent of the earth, whether upward or downward, / after that create offspring especially, O best of sages!"
Hearing his word, they went in all directions; / even today they do not return, like rivers from the ocean.
When the Haryaśvas had disappeared, Prajāpati Dakṣa again, / the lord, created a thousand sons upon Vīriṇī.
They were named Śabalāśvas, and gathered for the work of creation. / Nārada, the sage, again spoke to those who followed, just as before:
"Having known the full extent of the earth, and then your brothers, / coming back you shall create offspring especially."
They too went by that same path, following their brothers then. / Since then, a younger brother does not seek the path of the [elder] brother.
One who searches meets with sorrow; therefore one should avoid it. / Then, when they too had vanished, Prajāpati Dakṣa,
the son of Pracetas, then begot sixty daughters upon Vīriṇī. / He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, four to Ariṣṭanemi, / two to the son of Bhṛgu, and two to the wise Kṛśāśva,
and two to Aṅgiras he gave. Listen in detail to their names, / the mothers of the gods, and the expansion of their offspring from the beginning:
Arundhatī, Vasu, Jāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī, / Saṅkalpā, and Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and the lovely Viśvā—
these are declared the wives of Dharma; learn their sons from me: / The Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas;
the Marutvants were born of Marutvatī, and the Vasus of Vasu; / the Bhānus were born of Bhānu, and the Muhūrtajas of Muhūrtā;
those named Ghoṣas were born of Lambā, and Nāgavīthī of Jāmī; / whatever is born on the surface of the earth was born of Arundhatī;
from Saṅkalpā came Saṅkalpa. Behold the creation of the Vasus: / the luminous deities, who are all-pervading in all directions.
These are declared to be the Vasus; hear from me their names: / Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are renowned as the eight Vasus. / The sons of Āpa were four: Śrānta, Vaitaṇḍa,
and also Śānta, Muni, [and] Babhru, who are entitled to protect sacrifices. / Dhruva's son was Kāla, and Varcas was born from Soma.
Draviṇa and Havyavāha are traditionally remembered as the two sons of Dhara. / Then, enduring until the end of the kalpa, were Prāṇa, Ramaṇa, and Śiśira,
Manohara, and Dhava, and then Śiva—the sons of Hari (Vāyu). / Śiva [begot] a son, Manojava, who bestows unknown paths.
And Anala obtained sons endowed with qualities resembling fire. / Among them was Śākha and Viśākha; in the sacred texts [they are born] from the Self-born;
and [he is] the offspring of the Kṛttikās, hence remembered as Kārtikeya. / Pratyūṣa's son was the sage named Ṛbhu, and then Devala.
Viśvakarman was the son of Prabhāsa, the artisan lord of creatures, / [working] in palaces, houses, gardens, statues, ornaments, and the like,
and the architect of the gods for tanks, pleasure-groves, and wells. / Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata,
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Sureśvara, / Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—
these are declared to be the Rudras, the eleven lords of the gaṇas. / Of these mind-born [deities] bearing excellent tridents,
their sons are considered eighty-four crores, imperishable, / who act as lords of the gaṇas protecting all directions.
These sons and grandsons were born from the womb of Surabhi. / I shall [now] declare the sons, grandsons, and descendants of Kaśyapa by his wives:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, / Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā,
Kadrū, Khasā, and Muni; learn from me the sons born to them. / The gods who were the Tuṣitas in the period of the Manu Cākṣuṣa
are remembered as the twelve Ādityas in the Vaivasvata period: / Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman,
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumat, and Viṣṇu. / These thousand-rayed ones are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
Born from Kaśyapa, son of Marīci, these sons were the delight of Aditi. / The sons of the sage Kṛśāśva are remembered as the weapons of the gods.
These hosts of gods, my dear, in each manvantara / are born and dissolve away, and likewise in kalpa after kalpa.
Diti obtained two sons from Kaśyapa, so it is heard by us: / Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.

Likewise, four sons were born to Hiraṇyakaśipu:
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Saṃhlāda, and Hlāda.

The sons of Prahlāda were long-lived Śibi, Bāṣkali,
and Virocana as the fourth, and he obtained Bali as his son.
Bali had a hundred sons, O king, with Bāṇa as the eldest; / then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Vivasvat, Aṃśutāpana,
the one named Nikuṃbha, Gurvakṣa, Kukṣi, Bhauma, and Bhīṣaṇa. / There were many others as well; Bāṇa was the eldest and supreme in virtue.
Bāṇa had a thousand arms and was endowed with skill in all weapons; / pleased by his austerities, the trident-holder (Śiva) resided in his city,
and attained companionship as Mahākāla with that wielder of the Pināka. / Hiraṇyākṣa had a son named Andhaka by name,
and likewise Bhūtasaṃtāpana and Mahānāga. / From them arose seventy-seven crores of sons and grandsons,
mighty, huge-bodied, of various forms, and of great energy. / Danu obtained from Kaśyapa a hundred sons proud of their boons.
Vipracitti was the foremost among them, endowed with great strength; / Dviraṣṭamūrdhan, Śakuni, Śaṅkuśirodhara,
Ayomukha, Śambara, Kapila, Vāmana, / Marīci, Māgadha, Hari, Gajaśiras,
Nidrādhara, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, Śatakratu, / Indramitra, Graha, and Vajranābha,
Ekavastra, Mahābāhu, Vajrākṣa, Tāraka, / Asiloman, Puloman, and the great Asura Vikurvāṇa,
Svarbhānu, and Vṛṣaparvan—such were the sons of Danu. / Suprabhā was Svarbhānu's daughter, and Śacī was the daughter of Puloman.
Upadānavī was Maya's [daughter], as were Mandodarī and Kuhū; / Śarmiṣṭhā, Sundarī, and Caṇḍā were the daughters of Vṛṣaparvan.
Pulomā and Kālakā were both daughters of Vaiśvānara, / having many children and great strength, wives of the son of Marīci (Kaśyapa).
To the two of them there were sixty thousand Dānavas in the past; / the son of Marīci formerly fathered the Paulomas and Kālakhañjas,
who dwelt in Hiraṇyapura and could not be slain by men; / having obtained boons from the Four-faced [Brahmā], they were slain by Vijaya (Arjuna).
Vipracitti begot nine sons on Siṃhikā; / indeed, they are the thirteen nephews of Hiraṇyakaśipu:
Kaṃsa, Śaṅkha, O best of kings, Nala, Vātāpi, / Ilvala, Namuci, Khasṛma, Añjana,
Naraka, Kālanābha, Paramāṇu, / and the renowned Kalpavīrya, increaser of Danu's lineage.

In the lineage of the Daitya Saṃhlāda were the Nivātakavacas,
who could not be slain by any of the gods, gandharvas, serpents, or rākṣasas.
who, relying on strength, were slain by Arjuna on the battlefield. / Tāmrā brought forth six daughters from the seed of the son of Marīci:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugṛdhrī, Gṛdhrikā, and Śuci. / Śukī duly brought forth parrots and owls;
Śyenī [brought forth] hawks, and Bhāsī brought forth ospreys; / Gṛdhrī [brought forth] vultures, and Sugṛdhrī pigeons and other birds;
Śuci brought forth swans, cranes, ducks, and water-fowls. / These are declared to be the offspring of Tāmrā; hear about [those of] Vinatā:
Garuḍa, the best of winged creatures, and Aruṇa, the lord of birds, / and a daughter, Saudāminī, who is renowned in the sky.
Sampāti and Jaṭāyus were both sons of Aruṇa; / Sampāti's sons were Babhru and the very renowned Śīghraga;
Jaṭāyus's renowned sons were Karṇikāra and Śatagāmin; / innumerable were the sons and grandsons of those birds.
In Surasā there were formerly a thousand serpents; / Kadrū of good vows obtained a thousand thousand-headed [serpents].
The prominent ones among them, O tamer of foes, are known to be twenty-six: / Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭa, Śaṅkha, Airāvata, Kambala,
Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla, Padma, Aśvatara, Takṣaka, / Elāpatra, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Balāhaka,
Śaṅkhapāla, Mahāśaṅkha, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra of fair countenance, / Śaṅkharoman, Nahuṣa, Ramaṇa, Paṇin,
Kapila, Durmukha, and Patañjalimukha. / Endless were the sons and grandsons of all these,
who were for the most part burned in ancient times in the house of Janamejaya. / Krodhavaśā brought forth the group of Rākṣasas of good names;
a myriad of those fanged beasts met destruction by Bhīmasena. / [She brought forth] fanged beasts, jackals, crows, and the like; buffaloes, cows, and boars [were born from Irā].
Surabhi formerly brought forth the triad from Kaśyapa; / Muni brought forth the assembly of sages, and likewise the troop of Apsarases.
Likewise, Ariṣṭā gave birth to many Kinnaras and Gandharvas; / Irā brought forth all grasses, trees, creepers, and bushes.
Khasā, however, gave birth to Yakṣas and Rākṣasas by the millions. / These were the descendants of Kaśyapa, by hundreds and by thousands.
O Bhīṣma, this creation is remembered as belonging to the Svārociṣa Manvantara. / Then, O knower of dharma, Diti bore from Kaśyapa / forty-nine Maruts, who are beloved to all the gods.
